title: Subject-Verb Agreement
shortDescription: The single highest-yield error-spotting rule in the whole syllabus — every pattern examiners hide the real subject behind.
genZNote: The subject and verb are a duo act. If one goes singular, the other can't quietly switch teams behind its back.

sections.heading: The core rule
sections.body: A verb must agree in NUMBER (singular/plural) with its SUBJECT, not with any other noun that happens to sit near it. Most agreement errors in exams come from a long or unusual sentence hiding the true subject behind other nouns, phrases, or clauses — so the first job is always to strip the sentence down and ask: what is the REAL subject of this verb?

sections.heading: Intervening phrases don't change the subject
bullets: Phrases starting with 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'accompanied by', 'in addition to' do NOT make the subject plural: 'The manager, along with his staff, IS attending the meeting' (manager = singular subject; staff is just extra information).
A phrase beginning with 'of' after the subject doesn't change its number: 'The quality of the products IS excellent' (subject is 'quality', not 'products').

sections.heading: Either / Neither / Each / Every / indefinite pronouns
bullets: 'Either', 'neither', 'each', 'every', 'everyone', 'everybody', 'anyone', 'someone', 'nobody' are all grammatically SINGULAR, even when they sound like they refer to many people: 'Each of the students HAS submitted the assignment.'
'Either...or' / 'Neither...nor' — the verb agrees with the noun CLOSER to it: 'Neither the manager nor the employees WERE informed' (agrees with 'employees').
'Every' and 'each' before two nouns joined by 'and' still take a singular verb: 'Every boy and girl WAS present.'

sections.heading: Collective nouns, uncountable nouns, and plural-form singulars
bullets: Collective nouns (team, family, jury, government) take a singular verb as one unit, plural when acting as separate individuals (see Nouns and Pronouns for detail).
Nouns plural in form but singular in meaning take a SINGULAR verb: news, mathematics, physics, economics, measles — 'Mathematics IS my favourite subject.'

Nouns like 'scissors', 'trousers', 'spectacles', 'pliers' are always treated as plural: 'The scissors ARE on the table' — with 'a pair of' before them, the verb stays singular ('A pair of scissors IS on the table').

sections.heading: Other tricky subject patterns
bullets: Subjects joined by 'and' usually take a plural verb: 'Ram and Shyam ARE friends' — UNLESS they refer to a single person/idea: 'Bread and butter IS my breakfast' (one dish).
'A number of' + plural noun takes a PLURAL verb ('A number of students HAVE applied'); 'The number of' + plural noun takes a SINGULAR verb ('The number of students HAS increased').
Distances, amounts of money, and periods of time, when treated as a single unit, take a singular verb: 'Ten kilometres IS a long distance to walk.'
A sentence beginning with 'there is/are' or 'here is/are' — the verb agrees with the noun that FOLLOWS it, not with 'there/here': 'There ARE many reasons for this.'
Subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor' with no 'either/neither' still follow the nearer-noun rule.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The verb must agree in number with its true subject, no matter what other nouns, phrases, or clauses sit between them — the single most-tested error type in competitive English.
keyFacts: 'Along with', 'as well as', 'together with' don't pluralise the subject.
Each/every/either/neither/indefinite pronouns are singular even when they suggest many people.
'A number of' = plural verb; 'the number of' = singular verb.
'There is/are' agrees with the noun that follows, not with 'there'.

highYieldFacts: 'The manager, along with his team, is attending' — singular, because 'along with' doesn't add to the subject.
'A number of students have applied' vs 'The number of applicants has increased' — opposite verb numbers despite looking similar.
commonTraps: Matching the verb to the noun closest to it instead of the real subject when a phrase intervenes.
Treating 'each'/'every'/'either'/'neither' as plural because they imply multiple people.
Getting 'a number of' and 'the number of' backwards.
mustRemember: Cross out prepositional phrases and 'along with/as well as' clauses mentally before checking subject-verb agreement.
With 'either...or'/'neither...nor', the verb always matches the nearer noun.

confusedTerms.distinction: 'A number of' means 'several/many' and takes a plural verb. 'The number of' refers to a specific count/figure and takes a singular verb.

possibleQuestions: Spot the error: 'The quality of the mangoes are not good this year.'
Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the players nor the coach ___ (was/were) happy with the result.'
